Proletariat

proh-luh-TAIR-ee-ut · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Proletariat is the working class; the group of wage-earning workers, especially those without significant property or capital.

The economist argued that the modern proletariat looks very different from the factory workers of the 1800s, but still shares the same basic position in the economy.

Worked Example

The novel's opening chapter describes the exhausted proletariat pouring out of the textile mills at dawn, their wages barely enough to cover rent.

Proletariat refers to the working class as a whole group, not to any one individual worker -- it's typically used when discussing economics, history, or politics.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

working class: The working class is the everyday name for people who earn wages doing manual or industrial work. Proletariat is the same people seen through economics and political theory — a class defined by owning no capital, met in histories and manifestos rather than casual talk.

rank and file: The rank and file are the ordinary members of one organization — a union, a party, an army — as opposed to its leaders. The proletariat is far broader: an entire economic class across a whole society, not the membership of any single group.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aristocracy: a ruling class of people with hereditary titles and privilege

elite: a select group considered to be the best or most privileged

Where it sits · how strongly it splits people from elites — workforce → proletariat → masses

workforce vs. proletariat: Workforce is a neutral, everyday term for everyone who works, without proletariat's specific class and history-loaded meaning.

masses vs. proletariat: The masses reaches further than the proletariat: it sweeps in the whole general population as against any ruling elite, while the proletariat is specifically the wage-earning class.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — prolet

Root — prolet: offspring, progeny (from Latin proles, 'offspring' -- a Roman proletarius was counted by his children)

Suffix — -ariat

Suffix — -ariat: a group or class of people (Latin -arius, via French -ariat)

Put it together

Put it together: Proletariat combines prolet ('offspring,' from Latin proles) with -ariat ('a class of people'), since ancient Roman law counted the poorest citizens as contributing to the state only through having children -- a proletarius owned nothing else of value except future generations.

Use the root in a new word: prolific

Use the root in a new word: prolific: A prolific author -- one who produces many books -- shares proletariat's Latin root proles, since prolific literally means 'producing offspring or output.'
